title: Yom Kippur War
description: 1973 war between Israel and Arab states
wiki_lead:
The Yom Kippur War, also known as the 1973 Arab–Israeli War, the fourth Arab–Israeli War, the October War, or the Ramadan War (6–25 October 1973), was fought between Israel and a coalition of Arab states led by Egypt and Syria. Most of the fighting occurred in the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights, territories occupied by Israel in 1967. Some combat also took place in mainland Egypt and northern Israel.
The war started on 6 October 1973, when the Arab coalition launched a surprise attack across their respective frontiers during the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur, which coincided with the 10th day of Ramadan. The United States and Soviet Union engaged in massive resupply efforts for their allies (Israel and the Arab states, respectively), which heightened tensions between the two superpowers.
Egyptian and Syrian forces crossed their respective ceasefire lines with Israel, advancing into the Sinai and the Golan Heights. Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal in Operation Badr, establishing positions, while Syrian forces gained territory in the Golan Heights. After three days, Israel halted the Egyptian advance and pushed most of the Syrians back to the Purple Line. Israel then launched a counteroffensive into Syria, shelling the outskirts of Damascus. The Egyptian forces continued the advance into Sinai on 14 October to relieve the Syrian front which was coming under increasing pressure.
Israeli forces exploited the failed Egyptian advance to breach the Suez Canal, advancing north toward Ismailia and south toward Suez to sever the Egyptian Second and Third Armies, with some units pushing west. However, their advance met fierce resistance on all fronts. Both sides accepted a UN-brokered ceasefire on 22 October, though it collapsed the day after amid mutual accusations of violations. With the renewed fighting, Israel succeeded in advancing south, materializing the threat to the Third Army's supply lines, but failed to capture Suez. A second ceasefire on 25 October officially ended the conflict.
The Yom Kippur War had significant consequences. The Arab world, humiliated by the 1967 defeat, felt psychologically vindicated by its early and late successes in 1973. Meanwhile, Israel, despite battlefield achievements, recognized that future military dominance was uncertain. These shifts contributed to the Israeli–Palestinian peace process, leading to the 1978 Camp David Accords, when Israel returned the Sinai Peninsula to Egypt, and the Egypt–Israel peace treaty, the first time an Arab country recognized Israel. Egypt drifted away from the Soviet Union, eventually leaving the Eastern Bloc.

Background


Arab–Israeli conflict
The war was part of the Arab–Israeli conflict, an ongoing dispute that has included many battles and wars since the founding of the State of Israel in 1948. grok_lead: The Yom Kippur War (Hebrew: ×××××ª ××× ×××¤××¨), also known as the October War or Ramadan War, was a major Arab-Israeli conflict that erupted on October 6, 1973, when Egyptian and Syrian forces launched coordinated surprise attacks against Israeli positions in the Sinai Peninsula and Golan Heights, respectively, exploiting the Jewish holy day of Yom Kippur when much of Israel's military was on reduced alert. A coalition involving expeditionary contingents from Iraq, Jordan, Algeria, Morocco, Libya, Kuwait, Tunisia, Saudi Arabia, as well as non-Arab support from Cuba and North Korea, bolstered the Egyptian and Syrian efforts, marking a concerted attempt to reverse territorial losses from the 1967 Six-Day War. Initial Arab advances, facilitated by deception operations and effective use of anti-tank guided missiles and surface-to-air defenses against Israeli armor and air power, caught Israeli intelligence and leadership off-guard, resulting in heavy early losses and a severe test of Israel's rapid mobilization capabilities. Israel's full reserve mobilization and counteroffensives shifted the momentum by mid-October, with Israeli forces crossing the Suez Canal to envelop the Egyptian Third Army and advancing to within artillery range of Damascus, prompting superpower intervention including a U.S. airlift of munitions that proved decisive in sustaining Israel's operations amid an Arab oil embargo. Cease-fires mediated by the United Nations on October 22 and 24 ended major combat, though violations extended fighting until October 25, yielding an Israeli victory that restored pre-war lines with gains but at the cost of 2,688 Israeli fatalities and widespread equipment losses. The war exposed vulnerabilities in Israeli overconfidence stemming from 1967 successes, triggering domestic inquiries like the Agranat Commission and the resignation of Prime Minister Golda Meir, while diplomatically catalyzing disengagement accords and paving the way for the 1979 Egypt-Israel peace treaty under U.S. auspices, fundamentally altering Middle East alignments despite persistent Syrian enmity. Arab performance, particularly Egypt's limited canal crossing, demonstrated tactical improvements over prior conflicts but underscored limitations in sustaining offensives against a resilient defender, influencing global perceptions of Soviet-supplied weaponry's efficacy.
